site.name: Abhinav Pangaria
site.longBio: Engineer who takes a problem down to the primitive it is missing and builds that. Orchestration and verification harnesses that make an autonomous agent prove its work rather than report it. Cryptographic systems that stop a public ledger from naming who paid whom. Settlement backends where a retry is theft and there is nothing to roll back. Retrieval and data pipelines inside a bank's asset and wealth management division, where the bottleneck was never the model. Rust, Go, Python and TypeScript across five runtimes, most of it owned end to end from the contract up to the dashboard.
site.headline: I build resilient systems, from idea to production.
site.heroLine: Full-stack engineer across backend, infrastructure and the product on top. Previously JP Morgan Chase. Stellar SCF grantee.

identity.statement: I build systems that hold together on the worst day, not the best one.
paragraphs: Verification loops for coding agents. Spend control for agents that hold money. Private payments, on-chain credit, cross-border payroll. Different problems, one bias: toward the boring, exhausting middle of the stack.
Sole builder on two of these, lead architect and engineer on the rest. JP Morgan Chase, asset and wealth management. Stellar SCF grantee, five hackathon wins.

about.lead: I take a problem down to the primitive it is missing and build that, usually end to end, from the contract or protocol up to the dashboard someone actually looks at.
about.body: Lately that means agents: a shared graph so parallel coding agents know when the code under them changed, a loop that makes an agent prove its work, and a control plane that decides what an agent may spend before it pays. Before that, settlement backends, privacy on Stellar, and retrieval inside a bank.

projects.name: Loom
projects.tagline: A shared, live world model for parallel coding agents, kept in one graph.
projects.description: Parallel AI coding agents write code that passes alone and breaks when merged. Agent A changes a function's contract, agent B writes a new caller against the old one, git sees no conflict, and the tests fail only after the merge. Loom keeps the code's call graph, every agent's in-flight edits, function-level leases, decisions and test evidence in one FalkorDB graph. On every edit a CALLS traversal of one to three hops finds exactly the agents whose in-flight code depends on the change, and Loom tells them what changed under them, mid-work. Leases are an atomic Cypher compare-and-set: 50 agents making 10,000 attempts got zero double grants, against 2,332 with the check disabled. Test runs are tied to the body hash they ran against, so a later edit marks a claim stale and blocks it, and any symbol can be walked back through decision, task, agent, change and commit. Measured on the 36 STALE-bench Django task pairs with Claude Haiku, 108 real runs across blind, oracle and live: without Loom 0 of 36 merges passed, with Loom 24 of 36 did, including 12 of 12 signature changes. Most of the remaining failures are return-type changes, where the notice arrived and the model kept its own code anyway.

projects.name: Zidd
projects.tagline: An AI English coach for learners in India, from Class 2 chapters to the interview room.
projects.description: Zidd is an AI English coach built for learners in India, and it runs two products on one engine. School teaches NCERT-aligned English for Classes 2 to 5 across 47 authored chapters, with a placement diagnostic, teaching sessions, recaps, and reports a parent can read. Career runs communication drills, mock interviews and group-discussion simulations for job-seekers. Learners answer in their own words, with explanations in English, Hinglish or Hindi. Every answer goes through a LangGraph decision graph that scores it and picks the next teaching move: teach a new idea, bridge down when the learner is lost, strengthen, challenge once they have it, or redirect when the answer is fluent but off the question. Every loop is capped so nobody gets drilled forever, and progression runs on a streak of clean passes rather than a moving average, because an average that settles at 0.8 never crosses a strict 0.8 gate and soft-locks a learner who is getting it right. The reply streams token by token over SSE. Underneath, it is built to stay correct on a free tier: boot fails closed if the secret, database or schema is wrong, open-answer grading runs through a Postgres job queue that resumes after a crash, session starts and credit charges carry idempotency keys so a retry never double-charges, and a pool of Gemini keys rotates on rate limits. Reports only state progress the saved evidence supports, so an empty report says so instead of guessing.

projects.name: Guardian Kane
projects.tagline: The loop that makes an agent's "done" something it has to prove, not just say.
projects.description: Guardian Kane is a reviewed, phased, scope-guarded verification loop wrapped around Claude Code, not just a Stop-hook check (that's where it started; the current build spans twelve numbered phases). Every PRD use-case and generated test has to clear a review gate before it counts as real. A phased task tracker attributes every task, claim, and file to a build phase. Per-task verification then drives a real local browser through a scripted test plus an independent defect sweep before a task can advance to KANE_VERIFIED. Three failed attempts escalate to a human instead of looping forever. Underneath that: a local Jaccard-similarity bug-memory store, a real-time scope guard, a secret-scan security gate, file-level task locking, and a four-tab dashboard (code graph, memory graph, PRD graph with gaps & drift, live activity) with a chat bridge straight into the running agent. Proven across four paired A/B builds, including the flagship ORBITAL financial dashboard, where the unassisted baseline reported "done" on a doubled chart and an off-spec alerts layout, and the gated build shipped neither.

projects.name: AgentOps
projects.tagline: The organizational control plane for agents that hold money.
projects.description: A wallet gives an agent the ability to pay. AgentOps decides whether it is allowed to. Every agent is an explicit organizational identity with its own wallet, role, policy bindings and budget, and every economic action it attempts runs one fail-closed path: verify identity, evaluate policy, check budget, escalate to a human when a threshold is crossed, then execute, settle, and write an evidence record that links the agent's intent to its on-chain settlement. Money moves on Circle's infrastructure, with the rail chosen by the relationship: x402 and Gateway for machine-to-service commerce, Permit2 for bounded agent-to-agent spending, ERC-8183 escrow for a first interaction with an unproven counterparty, and ERC-8004 identity and reputation once the work completes. Agents reach the control plane over a hosted MCP server, the same one human operators govern. Demonstrated as a five-agent research organization across Arc Testnet and Base Sepolia: policy-controlled hiring, second-hop delegation where an agent hires another agent on its own authority, approval-gated cross-chain execution, and capital that can be revoked from an agent and recovered.

projects.name: Pods
projects.tagline: NIM-backed accountability for small groups. Commit, show up, earn, repeat.
projects.description: Pods is a NIM-backed accountability app for small groups on Nimiq Pay. Commit NIM upfront, submit proof for scheduled activities like shipping code, fitness, reading, or study, and get payouts proportional to your presence. The creator reviews proof but never funds or receives participant money, so every settlement stays deterministic and disclosed.

projects.name: VEIL
projects.tagline: Privacy as a wallet primitive. Shielded notes, private sends, and prediction markets on Stellar.
projects.description: A private wallet and prediction market built on Stellar testnet. Public USDC converts into spendable shielded notes, private note-to-note transfers, batch payouts, and market participation all run through the same note model, so privacy is part of the wallet flow rather than bolted on. A backend prover and relayer generate proofs, simulate transactions, and settle pool state on-chain.

projects.name: Kredio
projects.tagline: DeFi with memory. Polkadot's on-chain credit layer.
projects.description: A credit layer for Polkadot that scores a borrower from on-chain behaviour rather than an oracle feed, so there is no price or reputation input to manipulate and nothing to bribe. Scoring runs across two runtimes at once through hybrid EVM and PolkaVM atomic calls, and the resulting score travels between parachains over XCM, which means a borrower's history follows them instead of restarting on every chain.

projects.name: OpenAssets
projects.tagline: The Mantle-native gateway bridging the RWA liquidity gap.
projects.description: A fundamental Real-World Asset (RWA) execution layer. Built for the Mantle Global Hackathon, OpenAssets transforms off-chain cash flows into credit-enabled primitives. Featuring ERC-3643 (T-REX) compliance, mETH-powered leverage vaults, and 'Token-Day' engines to prevent yield sniping. A system built for the next cycle of institutional RealFi.

projects.name: PayZoll
projects.tagline: Cross-border payroll and treasury, built for crypto-native teams.
projects.description: Cross-border payroll and treasury for teams whose members all hold different assets. I was sole technical owner of the payment infrastructure on a two-person founding team. The Stellar Disbursement Platform went from single-tenant to a multi-tenant distributed system running batch payroll for many organizations at once, with signing keys derived in AWS KMS instead of stored as raw tokens and payroll records encrypted at rest with pgcrypto. The interesting constraint was throughput: SDP was capped at eight channel accounts, roughly two transactions per second. Soroban's authorization-tree model let a single channel account fan out into many parallel contract calls, which took it to about 200.

projects.name: Tesseract
projects.tagline: Privacy-preserving payment & identity mixing on Stellar.
projects.description: Deposit, wait, withdraw. Built to expand Stellar Disbursement Platform with Privacy, Tesseract severs the link between depositor and recipient. Featuring channel-account rotation and layered hybrid encryption, it ensures that the most boring path through the system is also the most private one.

episodes.title: The Polaris Signal.
episodes.subtitle: Shortlisted for Round 4 of India's most selective student fellowship.
episodes.excerpt: Out of thousands of applicants nationwide, shortlisted for Round 4, the final interview round of the Polaris Fellowship, for a shot at one of ten seats in Bangalore.

body.text: Thousands of students, builders, and researchers applied to the Polaris Fellowship 2026: India's most selective residential program, ten seats nationwide, six months embedded inside the country's sharpest startups and venture firms. Round 1 filtered the noise. Round 2 asked for an unscripted video: who are you beyond the resume, what have you actually shipped, what's the most ambitious thing worth building in the next ten years.
Phase 09 / Selection
Receipts, not roadmaps.

Round 3 changed the question: not what you plan to build, but what you've already built, in the trenches, where it broke and what no tutorial covered. The brief was to walk through one project in full technical depth: architecture, the hardest problem solved, and what would be done differently next time.
genuine depth on something real

Clearing Round 3's technical deep dive earned a place in Round 4, the final round: a thirty to forty five minute interview with the Polaris panel, the last filter before ten seats are named in Bangalore.

episodes.title: The Agentic Economy.
episodes.subtitle: Building the policy firewall for autonomous agent payments on Casper.
episodes.excerpt: AI agents are about to hold real spending power. AgentOps is the control plane that lets them build without handing over a blank check, proven live and anchored on-chain on Casper.

body.text: Autonomous agents are being handed real spending power before anyone builds them a conscience. An agent with a private key and no spend cap, no velocity limit, no kill-switch, and no tamper-proof record of what it did with the money it was given is unbounded risk. Today, the only insight into a misbehaving agent is a bank statement after the damage is done.
Phase 08 / Governance
A policy firewall, not a wallet.

AgentOps sits between the agent and the chain. Every payment, trade, and deploy an agent attempts is checked against operator-defined rules in real time: spend caps, velocity limits, destination scope, signed or denied on the spot, with a budget hold placed atomically so an agent can never double-spend against an in-flight payment.
Prove every decision forever on Casper, immutably and on-chain.

Once a decision settles, its hash is anchored to a custom Rust/Odra smart contract, the GuardRegistry, where re-anchoring the same hash is a no-op and submitting a different hash for an already-anchored decision causes the contract to revert. The audit trail cannot be rewritten later, not even by the team that built it.

episodes.title: Privacy as a Habit.
episodes.subtitle: Extending Tesseract's thesis into a full private wallet on Stellar.
episodes.excerpt: From a single private-payment mechanism to a complete wallet: shielded notes, private sends, batch payouts, and private prediction markets, all on Stellar.

body.text: Tesseract proved a mechanism: deposit, wait, withdraw, and the link between depositor and recipient disappears. It was one door. VEIL asks what happens when privacy needs to be the entire building: a wallet where every surface, not just the transfer, understands how to stay quiet.
Phase 07 / Continuity
One note model, every surface.

Public USDC converts into shielded notes on deposit. Those notes spend privately, split into change, batch into payouts, or convert into Market Notes for private prediction-market positions, all through the same commitment model, so the private path is never a special case bolted onto the public one. A backend prover and relayer generate proofs, simulate transactions, and settle pool state on Stellar testnet.
Privacy should be part of the wallet flow itself.

What shipped is a live client with wallet and market privacy pools, an encrypted client-side vault, deposit and withdrawal flows, note transfers, batch payments, and claimable market payouts: the same thesis as Tesseract, extended until it stopped being a primitive and became a product.

episodes.title: Privacy as Primitive.
episodes.subtitle: Building temporal decorrelation on Stellar.
episodes.excerpt: Deposit, wait, withdraw. A Distributor severs the link between depositors and recipients. The most boring path is the most private one.

body.text: Privacy as a feature is marketing. Privacy as a primitive is architecture. Tesseract makes that distinction concrete: a mechanism where a detached Distributor handles outflow, breaking the on-chain link between depositor and recipient. Channel-account rotation, hybrid encryption, and BullMQ-backed scheduling ensure that the system remains stable and private.
Phase 06 / Mastery
The silent protocol.

I came out of the Soroban season with a much narrower set of opinions and a much wider set of scars. Both compound. The result is a protocol that does one thing perfectly: it clears private payments without the theater of 'zero-knowledge' marketing.

episodes.title: RealFi Mastery.
episodes.subtitle: Bridging the RWA liquidity gap.
episodes.excerpt: From the U2U Vietbuild win to Mantle-native RWA layers. Moving beyond hackathon products to fundamental financial primitives.

body.text: OpenAssets found its niche in the gap between trade receivables and on-chain liquidity. We first proved the concept at the Vietbuild hackathon for U2U network, taking home the win. But a hackathon product is just a sketch. We redesigned and revamped the entire stack for the Mantle Network, focusing on ERC-3643 (T-REX) compliance and institutional-grade security.
Phase 05 / Primitives
The RWA Primitive.
If your protocol cannot handle compliant Real-World Assets with the precision of a legacy bank, you are playing a game. We built OpenAssets to be the fundamental service.

We implemented mETH-powered leverage vaults and universal credit abstraction (OAID). It was a season of high-stakes architectural decisions, transforming a 48-hour win into a cornerstone of the Mantle ecosystem.

episodes.title: The Bank Floor.
episodes.subtitle: Python, retrieval, and a bug queue that took a week.
episodes.excerpt: Three months inside JP Morgan Chase, Asset and Wealth Management. A RAG triage service written in Python that pulled bug resolution from about a week down to a day, and Snowflake pipelines that cut manual reporting by over 60% across the division.

body.text: A bank is where you find out what the word internal actually costs. In the Asset and Wealth Management division the bug queue had a shape everybody had stopped questioning: a ticket arrives, an engineer goes looking through Jira history and Confluence pages for the last time something like this happened, and about a week later it is resolved. Nobody was doing anything wrong. The knowledge simply was not retrievable.
Phase 04 / Retrieval
The fix was retrieval, not process.

I built the triage service from scratch in Python, served through FastAPI, with Confluence documentation and Jira ticket data as the corpus. Given a new ticket it returns the prior incidents that genuinely resemble it and the resolution path that worked on them. Bug resolution went from roughly a week to about a day.

The second half of the work was data movement rather than retrieval: real-time Snowflake pipelines on AWS, replacing reporting that people were assembling by hand, cutting that effort by over 60% across the division. Different problem, same lesson I keep meeting. Most of what looks like a people problem is an interface between two systems that nobody owns.

episodes.title: The Settlement Season.
episodes.subtitle: From the first prototype to a settled payment path.
episodes.excerpt: A prototype I built through an Open Campus incubation and a Stellar hackathon became an SCF-backed company. I owned the Stellar core: path formation, settlement, and the disbursement integration.

body.text: PayZoll began as a thesis on friction. Capital moves slowly between borders and blockchains. I was on it from the first prototype: through the Educhain Open Campus incubation, then the Stellar Build Better hackathon, then the build that carried the SCF application. A $100K grant from the Stellar Development Foundation turned that prototype into a company, and I stayed on the Stellar side of the engineering as a co-founder.
Phase 03 / Conviction
Engineering as a thesis.

I was the sole technical owner of the payment infrastructure, and the work was less glamorous than the pitch. Redesigning the Stellar Disbursement Platform from single-tenant into a multi-tenant distributed system. Moving signing keys out of raw token storage and into hardware-derived material in AWS KMS, so no organization's funds or data were ever exposed to another's. Rebuilding the transaction queue with distributed workers and a real-time event layer, because the old "optimistic done" status marked payments successful before on-chain confirmation, and a payment that lies about itself is worse than one that fails loudly. Then a fund-recovery service to unwind partial failures without losing funds.

The ceiling I remember best was arithmetic. The platform could hold eight channel accounts, which meant about two transactions per second, which meant a large payroll took longer than a payroll is allowed to take. Soroban's authorization-tree model turned out to allow one channel account to fan out into many parallel contract calls, and that moved it to roughly 200 per second. Rust and Go, learned as needed. The part that stayed with me is not any deploy, it is what a payment system has to get right at 3am on a Sunday, when there is nobody to reverse anything.

episodes.title: The Crucible.
episodes.subtitle: 4-day sprints and solo marathons.
episodes.excerpt: Four-day sprints and one solo marathon across Stellar, Polkadot, and Mantle. Where the habit of reading the protocol before writing the code got formed.

body.text: The arc reached its peak during the four-day Stellar Build Better hackathon. Entering as a newcomer, I took the high-risk path and solo-coded the infrastructure. The first twelve hours went into the core protocol docs rather than the editor, mapping a multi-hop path payment that converted assets mid-flow. It placed first, and the lesson that stuck was about the twelve hours, not the placement.
Phase 02 / The Operator
Systems that clear.
Winning is a byproduct of planning. From solo marathons on Stellar to hybrid EVM / Wasm logic on Polkadot, the goal was never just to 'finish', it was to build systems that clear under pressure.

The momentum shifted to Polkadot, where I built Kredio. New to Substrate, I implemented cross-chain credit scoring over XCM and it earned an Honorary Award. Then the Mantle Global Hackathon, where my team and I architected OpenAssets. What I took from both was narrower than a trophy: how a score computed from public history gets farmed, and why compliance has to live inside the transfer rather than in a document beside it.

The tally, for anyone counting: first at Stellar Build Better, a win at VietBuidl U2U, a win at the Mantle Global Hackathon, third at Pharos Builder Camp, and an honorary award from Polkadot for arriving at Substrate as a newcomer. Five placements across five different ecosystems, which is less a record than a description of how I learn a stack: build the hardest thing it allows, under a deadline, in front of people who know it better than I do.

episodes.title: The Apprenticeship.
episodes.subtitle: Theory meets the wire at IIIT.
episodes.excerpt: IIIT Guwahati, first semester. Writing malloc from scratch to understand segfaults, and a stubborn refusal to write throwaway code. Algorithms by day, Linux stacks at 2am.

body.text: College began as a race for technical depth. While the syllabus covered the basics, I was building my own detention center for bugs. Writing malloc from scratch to understand segfaults, scraping portals before there was a polite reason to, and obsessing over the distance between a textbook example and the actual wire.
Phase 01 / The Foundation
Learning to see the system.

What I was actually learning was the distance between a textbook example and the wire. Reimplementing things that already existed, badly at first, until the failure modes stopped being surprising. The path from a first-year exercise to a system other people depend on is not a leap, it is a thousand boring repetitions.
